Good morning again, Heads of State and Government, Mr. Chef de Cabinet of the Office of the Secretary General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I warmly welcome all of you to this high level meeting. Members will recall that by its resolution 68/32 of December 5th, 2013, the Assembly declared 26 September as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. In its resolution 79/47 of December 2nd, 2024, the General Assembly reiterated its request for the organization on September 26th every year a one-day high-level plenary meeting of the Assembly to commemorate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. Today, that meeting is being held. In addition, as delegations were informed in my letter dated September 16, 2025, in keeping with the spirit of General Assembly resolution 72/251, I have invited civil society representatives to make contributions to the meeting. It is my intention to invite these representatives to speak at the end of the afternoon meeting. The International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons is devoted to furthering the objective of mobilizing international efforts towards achieving the common goal of a nuclear weapon free world. including through enhancing public awareness and education about the threat posed to humanity by nuclear weapons and the necessity for their total elimination. Allow me now to make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Dear Excellencies, We did not create the United Nations 80 years ago because peace was a neutral state of humanity. From the moment we learned to fashion spears and blades, humanity turned tools into weapons. As those weapons grew more sophisticated, our wars grew more brutal, culminating into the total destruction of the last century. At Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in two blinding instance, humanity confronted a horrifying truth. We had acquired the ability to erase civilization itself. That is why we needed, this is why we built this organization, our United Nations. not only for the aspirations of multilateralism and cooperation, but as a guardrail against our most destructive instincts, a North Star to guide us away from the health of our own making. Yet, 80 years later, the scourge of war has not been eradicated. Besides all treaties, since Hiroshima and Nagasaki, more states have acquired nuclear weapons, while those that already possess them have expanded their arsenals. In theory, the world accepts that a nuclear war must never be fought and can never be won. Yet, that has not stopped some from building even larger arsenals. or even from repeatedly coming to the brink of using them. During the Cold War, false alarms, misread signals, and reckless standoffs nearly unleashed catastrophe, most famously during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Now the danger is more complex. What if terrorists acquire these weapons? What if artificial intelligence accelerates decision-making, leaving no room for human restraint? The risk of miscalculation today may be greater than at any point since 1945. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, managing these risks, especially in areas of disagreement, is precisely one of the tasks for which the United Nations was created. And as I said in my opening speech, it's not because we do not know our compass, it's not because our compass does not work, we do have effective frameworks for reducing nuclear dangers shaped by this organization. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and the Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaties. These are concrete guardrails. They build habits of restraint and keep doors open to deeper reductions. But as I also said on the opening speech, treaties alone are not enough. Member States, each Member State has to line up to them, has to live up to them. especially those who possess these monstrous weapons. The most simple thing would be to commit to policies of no first use. And rather than pouring resources into new arsenals, we should invest in the biggest security threat for all humankind of this century, the climate crisis. Just imagine if you would use all that money invested into nuclear weapons today for fighting exactly this, the climate crisis, the injustice of social divide. And we should also think about the potential of newer forms from this technology directed to serve humanity constructively and safely. Used wisely and under regulation, nuclear technology can, for example, diagnose and treat cancer, monitor oceans and the atmosphere. But also these civil technologies must be kept safe because civilian facilities, reactors, laboratories, universities, hospitals could also be turned into targets of war. again with dramatic consequences. And therefore we have to join forces to protect them wherever, whenever, to be better and safer together. Excellencies, we do not live in heaven. We live in the world we are living in. Therefore we must be pragmatic. Nuclear weapons exist. Indeed, tens of thousands of nuclear weapons exist. And whether we like it or not, deterrence and balance still feature in delicate security architectures. But they are not ends in themselves. While we cannot be naive about the world as it is, neither can we give up on the world as it should be. It's in our hands. And as I underlined in the opening of the general debate, To give up because we have tried and failed would be to let evil prevail. Our efforts must preserve not because of any certainty that we will win, but because we know it's the right thing to do. And we know that it's the right thing to do to disarm, to reduce the risk of likelihood of nuclear weapons ever being used. Durable security rests not in ever-growing arsenals, but in disarmament, in non-proliferation, and, one day, in abolition. Excellencies, two weeks ago, when together with the Secretary-General and the Japanese representatives, I rang the peace bell for the International Day of Peace, I recalled my visit to Nagasaki. Back there, I met schoolgirls. who told me why they are fighting for a nuclear weapon free world. Because they didn't experience the horrors of bombing themselves, but they inherited them through generations from their grandparents who, some of them were killed by the nuclear bombs and others had to live with the consequences for life. Those great-granddaughters of the victims have become fierce advocates for peace. They know with unsentimental clarity that humanity holds the power to erase civilization in a single reckless act. For their sake and for the memory of those reduced to shadows in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, let us resolve that their great-granddaughters and their great-grandsons will grow up one day in a world free of nuclear weapons. I thank you. I now give the floor to Mr. Courtney Vretray, Chief of Cabinet, who is representing Secretary General of the United Nations. Sir, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to join you today. I will share a message from the United Nations Secretary-General to mark this important occasion. Excellencies, we gather under a shadow that should have been lifted long ago, a threat born of human design and prolonged by human folly. Nuclear weapons continue to menace our world. And despite decades of promises, we see this threat accelerating and evolving. Last month, the world marked 80 years since the devastation of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Every day since then, the hibakusha, the survivors, turned their suffering into a call for peace. They were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize and have stirred the global conscience. And yet, every day, we see newer and even more dangerous weapons. Nuclear testing threats returning, norms eroding, dialogue fading, and the nuclear saber rattling louder than in past decades. Hard-won progress, reductions in arsenals, the cessation of testing, these are being undone before our eyes. We are sleepwalking into a new nuclear arms race, more complex, more unpredictable, and even more dangerous. New technologies and new domains of conflict have erased the margins for error. From cyberspace to outer space, from hypersonic missiles to deep sea drones, the risks of escalation and miscalculation are multiplying. This is not just a crisis of weapons, it is a crisis of memory, responsibility, and courage. That is why I have appointed an independent scientific panel to assess the effects of nuclear war. The panel has a mandate to ensure that our collective response to nuclear risk is grounded in rigorous scientific evidence. Excellencies, we must reject the myth that disarmament depends on the so-called right conditions. Article 6 of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty makes no such exception. Disarmament is not the reward for peace. It is the foundation of peace. We know the total elimination of nuclear weapons will not happen overnight. But it will never happen if we keep waiting for perfect conditions. So no more excuses. No more delays. No more ignoring legal obligations. No more abandoning future generations. States that possess nuclear weapons must return to dialogue. They must adopt and implement transparency and confidence-building measures to prevent catastrophic miscalculation. They must also ensure that humans always retain full responsibility and accountability for any decisions to use nuclear weapons. State parties must also honor their commitments under the NPT. I call on every state to ratify the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, ending once and for all and for all the dark legacy of nuclear tests. And every state must support the victims of nuclear use and testing and confront the enduring harm, poisoned lands, chronic illness, and lasting trauma. I urge the United States and the Russian Federation to negotiate further arsenal reductions. These steps alone will not build a world without nuclear weapons, but without them, we surrender our future to fear and silence the promise of peace. If we fall to now, we condemn future generations to live forever under the shadow of our mistakes. On this International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, let us make long needed progress to forge a world free of these weapons of extinction. Let us build that world together with courage, conviction and concrete action. I thank you.

Madam President, Excellencies, good morning. I have the responsibility to share the experiences of the Marshallese people, which informs the reality that nuclear weapons are an abomination and their very existence is a violation of human rights because they represent the utmost disregard for humanity. Between 1946 and 1958, 67 known nuclear weapons were tested on the Marshall Islands by the United States of America. The most infamous of these was the Castle Bravo test of March 1, 1954. At that time, we were under a UN trusteeship, administered by the United States and the UN Trusteeship Council allowed for these tests to take place. The Bravo shot caused the darkest day in the history of my people. Our human rights were so grossly violated on that day, and its consequences have carried through over the generations. Following the Castle Bravo test, the Marshallese people on neighboring atolls were exposed to nuclear fallouts and began to experience radiation sickness. Without their consent, they were subjected to a top secret experiment called Project 4.1 to study the effects of their exposure. We became sick with cancers, infertility, stillbirths, and the birth of jellyfish babies. a term used to describe children born without a skeletal structure and with translucence skin only to die shortly after. Our atolls became poisoned and even today there are Marshallese people that are displaced and unable to return to their ancestral lands due to the remaining radioactive contamination, undermining their right to self-determination. We continue to suffer the health effects of their nuclear legacy with high rates of cancer and other non-communicable diseases. Our right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment has been compromised, made worse by the nuclear waste dump left on Runit Island with the radioactive waste seeping into our lagoon due to climate change-induced sea level rise. For the Marshall Islands, the connection between nuclear disarmament and the protection and enjoyment of human rights is undeniable as we have lived experience that informs this understanding. We are testament to the reality that nuclear weapons cause human rights violations, as we have lived through those violations in the past. We are continuing to grapple with the challenges that persists to this day and we know that these will continue in the future. For the sake of humanity, we must unite on their complete elimination. I thank you.

For your kind attention.

At the outset, we would like to express our appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting and to the Secretary-General for his participation. The Non-Aligned Movement welcomes the commemoration of 26 September as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, designated through United Nations General Assembly Resolution 68/32. The movement considers the annual observation of this international day as an effective means of drawing the attention of the international public to the unacceptable dangers of nuclear weapons the concomitant necessity for their total elimination and the advantages of nuclear disarmament for development as well as for international peace and security. During the 19th summit of the Non-Aligned Movement held in January 24 in Kampala, member states reaffirmed the principal position that nuclear disarmament has been and remains the highest priority for the movement. the heads of state and government stressed that progress in nuclear disarmament and nuclear non-proliferation in all its aspects is essential to strengthen international peace and security. They also stressed the importance of ensuring that efforts aimed at nuclear non-proliferation are parallel to efforts aimed at nuclear disarmament. In this regard, we emphasize that the convening of the United Nations high-level International Conference on Nuclear Disarmament, as mandated by the relevant General Assembly resolutions, would provide an important opportunity to review progress made in nuclear disarmament and to further promote this noble objective. The NPT reaffirmed the importance of implementing the three pillars in a balanced manner. The slow progress towards nuclear disarmament and the nuclear weapons states' lack of progress towards accomplishing the total elimination of their nuclear arsenals in accordance with their relevant multilateral legal obligations and commitments remain issues of deep concern to the Dalai Lama movement. We affirm the need for urgent and concrete actions aimed at achieving this goal of nuclear disarmament. non state parties to the treaty reiterate the urgent need for accountability of the nuclear weapon states for their disarmament obligations under the ntp through benchmarks concrete, measurable, and time-bound actions on nuclear disarmament with established deadlines and reporting their implementation on these obligations to the review council until the goal of total elimination of nuclear weapons is achieved. The non-aligned movement further reiterates its concern that qualitative and quantitative improvements in existing nuclear weapons and the development of new types of nuclear weapons and provided for in the military doctrines of some nuclear weapon states, contravene the commitments made to diminish the role of nuclear weapons in their military and security policies, as well as the negative security assurances provided by the nuclear weapon states. The movement stresses once again that these improvements, as well as the development of new types of such weapons, violate also the commitments undertaken by the nuclear treaty states at the time of the conclusion of the Comprehensive Nuclear Treaty Ban and the NTP review conferences. The member states of the movement reaffirm the importance of the Conference on Disarmament as the single multilateral negotiating body on disarmament and call for the urgent commencement of their negotiations therein on further effective nuclear disarmament measures to achieve the total elimination of nuclear weapons including in particular on a comprehensive convention on nuclear weapons. We further call for urgent compliance with legal obligations and the fulfillment of commitments undertaken with regard to nuclear disarmament. To conclude, NAM welcomes the UN meetings and activities for the commemoration of the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons on this day, and we appreciate the participation of all delegations in this important event. We strongly encourage Member States, the UN system and civil society, including non-governmental organizations, academia, parliamentarians, the mass media and individuals to commemorate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons through all means of educational and public awareness-raising activities. I thank you, Mr. President, for this opportunity.

Madam President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the African Group. The Group associates itself with the statement of the Non Aligned Movement. Ladies and gentlemen, the African Group recalls the historic entry into force of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which supports the Vienna Plan of Action, as well as the conclusion of its third meeting of the States Parties. we await with great interest the upcoming review conference which will be chaired by south africa in two thousand and twenty six and we call upon nuclear weapon states and those under the nuclear umbrella to adhere to the treaty without delay. the african group also stresses the importance of a nuclear weapon free zone, namely the Treaty of N'Djamena, which reaffirms the commitment of Africa to remain a continent which is free of nuclear weapons. The modernization of nuclear arsenals, the use of the nuclear doctrine, as well as nuclear sharing agreements violate the spirit of the NPT. We underscore the importance of achieving a universal accession to the Treaty on the Complete Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, and we urge the States under Article 2 to sign the Treaty and to ratify it. We also recall at the disarmament conference and call upon the conference to emerge from the standstill in which it finds itself and to resume its substantive work. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, allow me to begin by expressing Lesotho's deep gratitude to you for convening this important meeting as we mark the 80th anniversary of the United Nations. This legacy reminds us of the urgency of preventing such devastation from ever recurring. The destructive impact of nuclear weapons and testing has never been confined to one region. Radioactive contamination poisons soils, rivers and oceans, with consequences that cross borders and generations. This shared vulnerability underscores the truly global nature of the threat. Mr President, Lesotho therefore stresses the urgent need to protect life on land and below waters. Instead of building trust, The stockpiling of arms amidst rising tensions only deepens mistrust and obstructs progress towards disarmament. The fragile environment risks reversing hard-won gains and undermines efforts to advance the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. I thank you, the Vice Minister for Political Affairs of Austria, for her statements. I now have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency, Levent Kumhurcu, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey. The floor is yours, sir.

So while commending Japan for the organization of the very sobering ceremonies in that regard, we believe it is our collective duty to honor the victims and ensure that such tragedies are never repeated. Turkey is fully committed to the ultimate goal of a world without nuclear weapons, while at the same time recognizing that there is no easy path to a nuclear weapon-free world. But we cannot give up or relent on this goal. In our mind, continued efforts toward a systematic, step-by-step, verifiable, and irreversible disarmament progress is not only a necessity, but it is our obligation. Turkey will continue to support all efforts in this regard, including the dialogue among the P5 countries. At the same time, it is becoming ever more critical to work on risk reduction efforts as well. Of course, this is not an alternative to efforts towards nuclear disarmament, but we have to ensure that nuclear weapons will never be used again, even while they exist. It is, of course, also critical to prevent further proliferation, which would make our common goal of a world without nuclear weapons even harder to attain. So we again underscore the fundamental importance of that Treaty of Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, which after 55 years remains the cornerstone of the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime, while recognizing the inalienable right of all state parties to enjoy peaceful use of nuclear energy. That said, Excellencies, the most recent attacks by a non-NPT state on nuclear facilities in an NPT state entailed many negative and dangerous ramifications, including on the implementation of NPT safeguards. So it is more urgent than ever to uphold our shared commitments and preserve the centrality and integrity of the NPT, which has no viable alternative. Looking towards the treaty's 11th review conference in 2026, it is the obligation of all states to ensure that the treaty remains intact, to strive for its universalization, and to fully implement their obligations, including, of course, Article VI. This is also in line with NATO's goal to forge a safer world for all and to create the security environment for a world while also, of course, underlining that as long as nuclear weapons exist, NATO will remain a nuclear alliance. Excellencies, in conclusion, that reiterates once again our commitment to achieve the ultimate goal of a world without nuclear weapons.

Thank you so much. I thank you, Mr. Deputy Prime Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey, for the statements. I now have the honor to give the floor to Her Excellency Ruth Cross Kwan Sing, Minister of Women, Youth, Sport and Social Affairs of Kiribati. It's yours, Madam.

Thank you, Chair. GDPS calls on all leaders and people of the world to renew commitments fostering greater cooperation and collaboration for a nuclear-free world, free of wars and rich in human fraternity, respect, trust, peace, harmony, and happiness as envisioned by the framers of the United Nations. Let's put our trust in the mechanisms of specific settlements of dispute. Thank you.

I thank the Minister of Women, Youth, Sports and Social Affairs of Kiribati for her statement. I now have the honour to give the floor to His Excellency Akan Rahmetulin, First Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

Thank you, Chair. This international day is built on the United Nations very first resolution in 1946, which called for the elimination of atomic weapons. Yet today, more than 12,000 nuclear warheads remain, many on high alert, while arms control frameworks that once provided stability are under severe strain. This day, therefore, is not only commemorative, but also a solemn call to urgent collective action. Kazakhstan's unwavering commitment to nuclear disarmament is based on a tragic legacy of more than 450 nuclear tests conducted at the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site. In response, we became the first nation to close such a site and voluntarily renounce the world's fourth largest nuclear arsenal. That decision was an act of principle, transforming tragedy into responsibility. It defines our national identity and our role as committed advocates of peace. We have since translated this principle into action. The Central Asian Nuclear Weapon Free Zone created jointly by the five countries of the region in 2006 will mark its 20th anniversary next year and prove that even a region bordering nuclear powers can choose mutual trust and cooperation. Last month in Astana, we convened this dedicated meeting on strengthening negative security assurances for all existing nuclear weapon free zones looking ahead the 2026 NPT review conference. Earlier this year, Kazakhstan presided over the third meeting of the States Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, where together with Kiribati, we actively promote victim assistance and environmental remediation, affirming that disarmament must also serve justice and humanity. Yet the dangers before us are worsening. The modernization of nuclear arsenals and the integration of artificial intelligence into the military domain introduce unprecedented risk of miscalculation and catastrophic escalation. Humanity must not allow technological innovation to become a source of even greater existential insecurity. The path forward is clear. Nuclear armed states, at the bare minimum, must reduce the role of these weapons in their doctrines, lower their operational readiness, cease any further buildup, and return to the fullest fulfillment of their disarmament obligations. the CTBT must finally enter into force. The NPT, the cornerstone of the global disarmament and non-proliferation.

Architecture, which has been gravely undermined by the continued threats posed by the existence of nuclear weapons. Ochoa.

Minister of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala for her statement. I now have the honor to give the floor to his Excellency Maxim Ryzhenkov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Belarus.
